title: The Spice Islands — The Age of Exploration, Chapter 1
eyebrow: CKHG Grade 5 · The Age of Exploration · Chapter 1 · Student Reader pp. 2–9
bigQuestion: According to the author, how did the search for the Spice Islands change history?

missions.name: What happened
missions.blurb: One question for each of the ideas this chapter is built on. The card says which page of the book answers it, and a wrong answer opens that page.

items.hi: but also as a way to preserve it

vs.q: Besides adding flavor, what did medieval Europeans need spices for?
opts: Keeping food from going rotten before it was eaten
Making the cloth dyes that colored their clothes
Keeping away the diseases that spread in the towns
Feeding the animals that were kept through the winter
vs.why: There was no refrigeration of any kind, so food had to be preserved some other way. That is why spices were worth so much trouble: not taste, but keeping meat safe to eat.

vs.q: Why did medieval Europeans need spices in a way that we do not?
opts: They grew nothing else that would season food
They had no refrigerators or other cold storage
They were not allowed to salt their own meat
They had no ovens, so food was eaten raw
vs.why: We keep food cold; they could not. Spices extended the time meat and other foods could be stored and still safely eaten, which is a job we now give to a machine.

vs.q: The chapter says spices were very expensive in Europe. Why?
opts: European rulers put a heavy tax on every spice sold
The plants had almost died out and were nearly gone
They grew in faraway Asia, and the trip was dangerous
Only a few cooks in Europe knew how to use them
vs.why: Distance and danger, not scarcity of the plants themselves. The spices grew in quantity — they were simply a very long and risky journey away, and everything that journey cost ended up in the price.

vs.q: What does the author say Europe's desire for cheaper spices set off?
opts: The end of the Middle Ages across Europe
A long war between Venice and the Arab traders
The building of the first ships that could cross oceans
The Age of Exploration and the settling of the Americas
vs.why: This is the Big Question in one sentence. Wanting the same spices for less money is what sent Europeans out across the oceans — and the author traces the settling of the Americas back to it.

opts: In present-day Indonesia, in Southeast Asia
Off the western coast of Africa
In the Caribbean Sea, west of the Atlantic
Along the southern coast of India
vs.why: Indonesia, on the far side of Asia from Europe. Everything else in the chapter follows from how far away that is.

vs.q: The Malay Archipelago stretches between which two places?
opts: From Arabia to the coast of Egypt
From the Malay Peninsula to Australia
From India across to eastern Africa
From southern China to the islands of Japan
vs.why: A chain of more than thirteen thousand islands running from the Malay Peninsula in Southeast Asia all the way down to Australia. The Spice Islands are a small part of it.

vs.q: What is the Ring of Fire?
opts: A belt of hot, dry desert along the equator
A warm ocean current that circles the Pacific
An arc of volcanoes around the Pacific Ocean
The yearly sailing route used by Arab traders
vs.why: An arc of volcanoes right around the Pacific. The Spice Islands sit on it because they lie where two sections of Earth's crust meet.

vs.q: What does sitting on the Ring of Fire do for the Spice Islands?
opts: It keeps them cool enough to grow spices all year
It gives them volcanoes, earthquakes, and rich soil
It makes the sea around them too rough for ships
It gives them a long dry season every single year
vs.why: Volcanic soil is rich soil. Put that together with the heat and the heavy rainfall near the equator and you get the exceptional spice crops the whole chapter is about.

vs.q: How did spices actually get from the Spice Islands to Europe?
opts: Venetian merchants sailed east and bought them at the islands
European ships rounded Africa and collected them each year
Arab traders carried them west and sold them to Venetians
They were carried overland the whole way by Mongol riders
vs.why: Two separate journeys and two separate sets of people taking a profit. No European ship had yet gone round Africa, so no European bought at the source.

vs.q: Where did the Arab traders hand the spices over to the Venetians?
opts: In Egypt
At the Spice Islands
In Venice
On the coast of India
vs.why: The Arab route ran round the Arabian Peninsula, up the Red Sea and north into Egypt. That is where the spices changed hands, and where the Arab traders took their huge profits.

items.hi: inspired European mapmakers to update their maps

vs.q: How did Marco Polo's book change things for Europeans?
opts: It gave sailing directions straight to the Spice Islands
It proved to Europeans that the Earth was round
It listed the prices the Arab traders were charging
It described Asian lands no European had written about before
vs.why: He was the first European to write about China, Thailand and the Malay Archipelago. Mapmakers redrew their maps because of it — which is a long way from giving directions, since the location of the Spice Islands was still a secret.

vs.q: Who did the chapter say was inspired by Polo's book two hundred years later?
opts: Christopher Columbus
Kublai Khan
The merchants of Venice
The Arab traders of Egypt
vs.why: An Italian sea captain reading a two-hundred-year-old book is the link the chapter draws between wanting spices and crossing the Atlantic. That is how the search for the islands ends up changing history.

missions.name: The words of the chapter
missions.blurb: The three words this chapter is built on — what each one means, and what it is doing here. Miss one and the book opens at the word with its definition.

vs.q: The chapter keeps saying medieval Europe. What does medieval mean?
opts: Relating to the Middle Ages in Europe
Living in the countryside rather than a town
Belonging to a time before anyone could write
Having to do with ships and sailing
vs.why: The Middle Ages, roughly the 400s to the 1400s. Every fact in this chapter sits inside that stretch of time, which is why the word turns up in the first sentence.

vs.q: Why does it matter that this chapter is about medieval Europe and not Europe today?
opts: Europe had no ships of any kind at that time
Nobody in Europe could read or write then
There was no way to keep food cold then
Europe and Asia were at war the whole time
vs.why: Change one thing — refrigeration — and the chapter stops making sense. Spices were worth a dangerous journey halfway round the world because there was no other way to keep food.

items.hi: preserve their monopoly of the spice trade

opts: A tax charged on goods brought into a country
Complete control of the supply of a good or service
An agreement between two countries to share a trade
A place where people come to buy and sell goods
vs.why: Complete control. The last answer is a trading center, which is a different word from this same chapter — worth keeping apart, because the Arab traders used trading centers to hold their monopoly.

vs.q: Arab traders told stories of monsters guarding the Spice Islands. How did that protect their monopoly?
opts: It explained to buyers why the spices cost so much
It frightened the Venetians into paying higher prices
If nobody else dared go, nobody else could supply the spices
It kept their own sailors from leaving to work elsewhere
vs.why: A monopoly lasts only while nobody else can reach the supply. For three hundred years the stories, and the secret location, did that job.

items.hi: could set whatever prices and taxes they pleased

vs.q: This chapter calls the Arabs traders and the Venetians merchants. Which is right?
opts: The Venetians were the traders and the Arabs the merchants
Both words are used for the Arabs only
Both words are used for the Venetians only
The Arabs were the traders and the Venetians the merchants
vs.why: Both words mean somebody who buys and sells. The chapter gives one to each end of the route: Arab traders brought the spices as far as Egypt, and Venetian merchants took them on into Europe.

vs.q: Once the Venetian merchants had the spices, what were they able to do?
opts: Sell them only to other merchants, never to families
Set whatever prices and taxes they pleased
Sell them only inside the city of Venice itself
Send any they could not sell back to the traders
vs.why: Anyone in Europe who wanted spices had to come to Venice, so Venice named the price. That made the city very wealthy and, the chapter adds, very unpopular.

why.title: Why spices mattered so much
vocab: relating to the Middle Ages in Europe
a plant used to add flavor to food
text: Supermarkets today stock all sorts of spices that can be used to season or add flavor to different foods. In medieval Europe, however, people relied on spices not only to flavor their food, but also as a way to preserve it.
Without refrigerators or other cold storage, medieval Europeans used spices to extend the time period during which meats and other foods could be stored and then safely eaten before turning rotten.

cost.title: Hard to get, and so very expensive
text: In the Middle Ages, spices were hard to get. Pepper, cinnamon, ginger, cloves, and other seasonings were grown in faraway Asia.
Getting the spices to Europe took a lot of time and effort. Distances were great, and travel back and forth was dangerous. As a result, spices were very expensive.
Europe's desire for cheaper spices sparked the Age of European Exploration and its settlement of the Americas.

islands.title: Where the Spice Islands are
text: Different spices come from different places. Many of the most desirable spices come from the islands of present-day Indonesia.

Indonesia is an archipelago , or chain of islands. It stretches from Southeast Asia's Malay Peninsula to the continent of Australia. This group, known as the Malay Archipelago, contains more than thirteen thousand islands.
Of all the spice-bearing islands, the Maluku Islands are probably the most famous. Indeed, for many years, Europeans referred to them as the Spice Islands.

fire.title: Volcanoes, rain, and very good spices
vocab: an area that gets less rain because it is on the protected side of a mountain
text: The islands of the Malay Archipelago are special. They mark a boundary between two sections of Earth's crust. The ridge formed by those sections is noted for its volcanoes and earthquake activity. It is part of the Ring of Fire, an arc of volcanoes that surrounds the rim of the Pacific Ocean.

Daytime temperatures are between 70 and 90 F year-round. Rainfall can be as much as 320 inches a year on the forested mountain slopes. On the rain shadow sides, it can be less than twenty inches a year.
Heat, heavy rainfall, and rich soil result in exceptional spice crops.

secret.title: A secret worth guarding
vocab: related to controlling the movement of a ship
a person who buys and sells goods
a situation in which one person, country, or company has complete control of the supply of a good or service
a place where people buy and sell goods
text: They did not yet know that the Atlantic Ocean went as far as the southern tip of Africa. Nor were their ships and navigational skills suited to such long voyages. And at the time, the exact location of the Spice Islands was a closely guarded secret.

For hundreds of years, from around 1100 until 1400, the Arabs managed to keep the location of the Spice Islands a secret. They even made up stories about how dangerous it was to sail to these islands.

If you had been alive then you might have heard tales told by Arab traders of the fantastic monsters and hideous flesh-eating birds that guarded the Spice Islands. Stories like these were designed to help the Arab traders preserve their monopoly of the spice trade.

route.title: How the spice trade worked
vocab: a person who buys and sells goods to earn money
text: How did the spice trade work? Arab traders sailed east to trading centers in India, Ceylon (now Sri Lanka), and the Spice Islands. After loading up their ships, they sailed west again.

A typical trip took them around the Arabian Peninsula, into the Red Sea, and north to Egypt. There they sold the spices to merchants from Venice and other parts of Italy. The Arab traders made huge profits from this exchange.

venice.title: Why Venice grew rich, and disliked
vocab: to discuss the terms of an agreement
text: The Venetians did well, too. They negotiated with Arab traders to distribute spices throughout Europe. Europeans wanting to purchase spices had to deal with Venice.
Once they had acquired the spices, the Venetian merchants could set whatever prices and taxes they pleased. This arrangement made Venice a very wealthy city. It also made the Venetians unpopular.
Wealthy Europeans had become used to exotic goods from the Venetian marketplace. At the same time, they resented the high cost of doing business with Venetian merchants.

polo.title: Marco Polo, and the book he told in prison
vocab: a native of the Asian nation of Mongolia
a group of people who serve as representatives of their government in another country
text: At the time, the Mongols controlled much of Asia and part of Europe. The Mongols made the roads safe for travelers, and many adventurers were anxious to seek their fortunes. Some went to trade for silk, gems, porcelain , and tea.
Kublai Khan took a liking to Marco. He sent Marco to distant parts of his kingdom on diplomatic missions . Wherever he went, Marco observed, asked questions, and remembered what he had seen.
During his days in prison, Polo talked about his travels, and the writer wrote down what Marco said. Together, the two cellmates produced a book that helped change the world.

Polo was the first European to write about China, Thailand, the Malay Archipelago, and other Asian lands. His book inspired European mapmakers to update their maps. Almost two hundred years after it was written, this book inspired an Italian sea captain named Christopher Columbus.
